problem: Existing visual target (object-goal) navigation methods are mostly single-robot and lack common-sense reasoning, so exploration in large or complex environments is inefficient and fragile. Multi-robot baselines rely on geometric heuristics or trained policies that do not generalize.
motivation: Multiple robots can cover large unknown environments faster and tolerate individual mistakes, but assigning robots to frontiers well needs semantic common sense. VLMs carry world knowledge and can reason over rendered maps zero-shot, so they are a natural global coordinator for multi-robot target search.
key_idea: Merge all robots' RGB-D observations into a shared global semantic 3D/top-view map, then use GPT-4o with frontier-marked visual prompts as a global planner that assigns a distinct frontier to each robot, while a local FMM planner handles low-level control.
insight: Semantic top-view context and VLM scale both matter: replacing the colored top-view map with an obstacle-only map drops SR from 0.666 to 0.645, and swapping GPT-4o for GPT-4o-mini drops SR to 0.641 and SPL from 0.368 to 0.307. Using two robots rather than one raises SR from 0.579 to 0.666 and SPL from 0.211 to 0.368. Random long-range goal sampling (SR 0.636) beat cost-utility (0.625), showing that spreading robots out matters, and the VLM adds semantic relevance on top of that.
method: Local/global 3D point cloud map: per robot, YOLOv8 detection plus Mobile-SAM segmentation, projected with depth and pose into a point cloud; all robots' maps merged into one global map and denoised with DBSCAN.

2D exploration map: 24x24 m at 0.05 m resolution, with obstacle and explored channels. Frontiers come from explored-area contours minus the dilated obstacle edge, clustered by connected components, with small clusters discarded.

Visual prompt: a colored top-view render of the global point cloud, with each robot marked by a circle and ID. One image is produced per candidate frontier, masked with that frontier and labeled with its ID.
Textual prompt: task, context, requirements (understand/analyze/decide/justify) and I/O format; the target category is given and GPT-4o returns a JSON mapping each robot to a frontier ID.

Decision making: the VLM is used only for global goal assignment, balancing collaborative exploration and semantic relevance to the target. Goals are refreshed every 25 local steps, with random explored points as fallback when no frontier exists.
Local policy: Fast Marching Method path planning to the assigned goal, with a short-range local goal converted to discrete actions.

Real-world deployment: two Unitree Go2 robots with RealSense D455 and Livox Mid-360, FAST-LIO2 localization, Generalized-ICP for initial inter-robot alignment; perception and VLM run on an RTX 4090 workstation at about 5 FPS.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen, via API) as global planner; YOLOv8 + Mobile-SAM for perception; FMM local planner
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D 480x640 + odometry/pose + goal category, per robot (2 robots)
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: move_forward 25 cm, turn_left/right 30°, look_up, look_down, stop; VLM chooses frontier goals globally
setting.privileged: none (robots start at the same position; poses given/estimated)

numbers.extra: multi-robot (2 robots), success if any robot finds the target; 500 steps per robot; 36 val scenes / 1000 episodes; 6 goal categories; success within 0.1 m as defined in paper

numbers_note: Multi-robot HM3D ObjectNav with a custom protocol (any robot succeeding, 2 robots, 6 categories); not directly comparable to the standard single-agent HM3D-ObjNav leaderboard. Split is described as validation (36 scenes, 1000 episodes).
results: Co-NavGPT reaches SR 0.666, SPL 0.368, DTG 1.684 on HM3D, beating the strongest baseline (Random Sample on Map: SR 0.636, SPL 0.336; Cost-Utility has DTG 2.030, Random Sample 2.048), Multi-SemExp (0.612 SR) and Greedy (0.611). Ablations show gains from multi-robot, semantic top-view maps and the larger VLM; real-world tests with two Go2 robots succeeded in three target searches (sink, person, chair).
limitations: Failures come from detection errors (~20%) and exploration issues (~14%: topological holes, absent target, multi-floor scenes); no multi-floor navigation.
Depends on a cloud GPT-4o API and a workstation GPU, with no closed-loop replanning or dynamic interaction; only 2 robots were tested; the real-world evaluation is qualitative only.
Absolute gains over simple baselines are modest (~3-5 SR points over random sampling).
